title: Interactions of several single nucleotide polymorphisms and high body mass index on serum lipid traits.
text_summary: 本研究旨在探讨10个单核苷酸多态性（SNPs）与高体重指数（BMI）对血清脂质特征的影响。通过对978名正常BMI和751名高BMI的百色瑶族人群进行基因分型和血脂检测，发现rs2070895和rs505151的基因型和等位基因频率在正常BMI和高BMI人群中存在显著差异。此外，rs2000813和rs3757354的基因型和等位基因频率也存在差异。在正常BMI人群中，TC、ApoA1（rs2066715）、TC、LDL-C、ApoA1、ApoB和ApoA1/ApoB（rs2070895）、TG、HDL-C和ApoA1（rs2000813）、TC、HDL-C、LDL-C、ApoA1和ApoB（rs1801133）以及HDL-C和ApoA1（rs3757354）的水平在不同基因型之间存在差异。在高BMI人群中，LDL-C、ApoB和ApoA1/ApoB（rs2066715）、HDL-C、ApoA1、ApoB和ApoA1/ApoB（rs2070895）、TC、HDL-C、ApoA1和ApoB（rs2000813）、TC、TG、HDL-C、LDL-C、ApoA1和ApoB（rs1801133）、TC、TG和ApoB（rs3757354）、TG（rs505151）、TG和ApoA1和ApoB（rs2016520）以及TC、HDL-C、LDL-C、ApoA1和ApoB（rs5888）的水平在不同基因型之间也存在差异。结果表明，rs2066715、rs2070895、rs2000813、rs1801133、rs3757354、rs505151、rs2016520和rs5888等SNPs与高BMI相互作用，影响血清脂质水平。这些发现表明，正常BMI和高BMI人群之间血清脂质水平的差异可能部分归因于多个SNPs与高BMI之间的不同相互作用。

Abstract
The interactions between single nucleotide polymorphisms
(SNPs) and high body mass index (BMI) on serum lipid proﬁles
are limited. This study was undertaken to detect the interac-
tions of 10 SNPs and high BMI on serum lipid traits in an iso-
lated population. A total of 978 normal BMI (<24 kg/m2) and 751
high BMI (24 kg/m2) subjects of Bai Ku Yao were randomly
selected from our previous stratiﬁed randomized cluster sam-
ples. Genotypes of rs2066715, rs1044925, low density lipopro-
tein receptor (LDL-R) Avak, rs2070895, rs2000813, rs1801133,
rs3757354, rs505151, rs2016520, and rs5888 SNPs were deter-
mined by polymerase chain reaction and restriction fragment
length polymorphism combined with gel electrophoresis, and
then conﬁrmed by direct sequencing. The interactions were
detected by factorial design covariance analysis. The genotypic
and allelic frequencies of rs2070895 and rs505151 were differ-
ent between normal and high BMI subjects, the genotypic fre-
quency of rs2000813 and allelic frequency of rs3757354 were
also different between normal and high BMI subjects (P < 0.01).

1. Introduction
Dyslipidemia such as elevated levels of total cholesterol (TC)
[1], triglyceride (TG) [2], low-density lipoprotein cholesterol
(LDL-C) [3], and apolipoprotein (Apo) B [4], together with
decreased levels of ApoA1 [4] and high-density lipoprotein cho-
lesterol (HDL-C) [5] has become a serious public health prob-
lem in many countries because of its high prevalence and a
causal relationship with serious medical condition such as cor-
onary artery disease (CAD), hypertension, and stroke [6]. It is
well known that dyslipidemia is a complex trait caused by
multiple environmental and genetic factors and their interac-
tions [7–12]. Although the associations between overweight/
obesity and dyslipidemia have been well documented [13–17],
information on the interactions between single nucleotide poly-
morphisms (SNPs) and high body mass index (BMI) on serum
lipid proﬁles is still scarce [18–21].
Bai Ku Yao (White-trouser Yao), an isolated subgroup of
the Yao minority in China, is named so because all of men
wear white knee-length knickerbockers. Because of isolation
from the other ethnic groups, the special customs and cultures
including their clothing, intra-ethnic marriages, dietary pat-
terns, and corn wine and rum intakes are still completely pre-
served to the present day. Thus, Bai Ku Yao is a useful sub-
group
for
population
genetic
studies.
In
previous
epidemiological studies, we found that the prevalence of dys-
lipidemia was lower in normal BMI than in high BMI subjects
[7–9]. We hypothesized that the differences in serum lipid lev-
els between normal and high BMI subjects might partly result
from different interactions of some SNPs and high BMI in this
population. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to detect
10 SNPs in different lipid-related genes and evaluate their
interactions with high BMI on serum lipid levels in the Guangxi
Bai Ku Yao population.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Study Population
This study consisted of 1,729 unrelated participants of Bai Ku
Yao who reside in Lihu and Baxu villages in Nandan County,
Guangxi, People’s Republic of China. They were randomly
selected from our previous stratiﬁed randomized cluster sam-
ples [7–9]. The age of the subjects ranged from 15 to 86 years,
with an average age of 41.38 6 14.71 years. There were 978
normal BMI (490 males and 488 females) and 751 high BMI
subjects (378 men and 373 women). All of the subjects were
rural agricultural workers. The subjects had no evidence of
diseases related to atherosclerosis, CAD, and diabetes. The
participants were not taking medications known to affect se-
rum lipid levels (lipid-lowering drugs, beta-blockers, diuretics,
hormones, or contraceptive drugs). The protocol was approved
by
the
Ethics
Committee
of
the
First
Afﬁliated
Hospital,
Guangxi Medical University. Written informed consent was
obtained from each participant.
2.2. Epidemiological Survey
The survey was done according to standardized methods [7–
9]. Questionnaires were administered to assess demographic
information, socioeconomic status, lifestyle factors, and medi-
cal and medication history. Blood pressure was measured
three times by a well-trained physician with the use of a
standard mercury sphygmomanometer while subjects were
seated and had rested for 5 min. Weight was measured with a
beam balance and height with a ﬁxed stadiometer. Subjects
were measured without shoes and in a minimum of clothing.
BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the
square of height in meters. Waist circumference was meas-
ured at the umbilicus.
2.3. Biochemical Measurements
Fasting venous blood samples of 5 mL were obtained from all
subjects. A part of the sample (2 mL) was collected into glass
tubes and used to determine serum lipid parameters. Another
part of the sample (3 mL) was transferred to tubes with antico-
agulate solution and used to extract deoxyribonucleic acid
(DNA). The levels of TC, TG, HDL-C, and LDL-C in samples
were determined by enzymatic methods. Serum ApoA1 and
ApoB levels were detected by the immunoturbidimetric immu-
noassay. All determinations were performed with an autoana-
lyzer (Type 7170A; Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan) in our Clinical Sci-
ence Experiment Center [7–9].
2.4. Genetic Analyses
Genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood leuko-
cytes by the phenol–chloroform method [10–12]. Genotyping of
rs2066715, rs1044925, low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-

rs1801133,

rs505151, rs2016520, and rs5888 was performed using poly-
merase chain reaction and restriction fragment length poly-
morphism (PCR-RFLP). The SNPs were selected according to
the previous ﬁndings of genome-wide association studies [22–
24] and bioinformatics functional assessment. Computational
analysis of 10 SNPs (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/SNP/buildhis-
tory.cgi) ascribed potential functional characteristics to each
variant allele. In addition, the 10 SNPs selected for genotyping
also based on the frequency of Beijing Han population from
the Human Genome Project Database. The heterozygosity val-
ues were higher than 10% for the minor allele frequency [25].
The sequences of the forward and backward primers and
restriction enzyme used for the genotyping of 10 SNPs, the

2.6. Diagnostic Criteria
The normal values of serum TC, TG, HDL-C, LDL-C, ApoA1,
ApoB levels, and the ratio of ApoA1 to ApoB in our Clinical
Science Experiment Center were 3.10–5.17, 0.56–1.70, 1.16–
1.42, 2.70–3.10 mmol/L, 1.20–1.60, 0.80–1.05 g/L, and 1.00–
2.50, respectively. The individuals with TC > 5.17 mmol/L and/
or TG > 1.70 mmol/L were deﬁned as hyperlipidemic [7–9].
BMIs < 24, 24–28, and >28 kg/m2 were deﬁned as normal
weight (normal BMI), overweight, and obesity (high BMI),
respectively [14].
2.7. Statistical Analysis
Data are presented as means 6 SD for continuous variables
and as frequencies or percentages for categorical variables.
Chi square tests were used to compare the differences in per-
centages and to assess Hardy-Weinberg expectations. Differen-
ces in mean values were assessed using analysis of covariance
(ANCOVA) and unpaired t tests. Potential confounding factors
included sex, age, education level, physical activity, blood
pressure, alcohol consumption, and cigarette smoking. All sig-
niﬁcant associations were further corrected for multiple tests
by a permutation test. The permutation test was conducted by
changing the orders of dependant variable randomly against

was repeated 1,000 times. The P values of 1,000 permutations
were sorted in a descending manner. If the observed P value is
less than or equal to the 950th P value, the association was
considered statistically signiﬁcant. The allelic and genotypic
frequencies

on serum lipid levels were assessed by using a factorial design
covariance analysis after controlling for potential confounders.

4. Discussion
In this study, we showed that the levels of serum TC, TG,
LDL-C, ApoA1, and ApoB were higher, and the levels of serum
HDL-C and the ratio of ApoA1 to ApoB were lower in high BMI
than in normal BMI subjects. This is in agreement with those
of previous studies in obese subjects [13–17]. The primary dys-
lipidemia related to obesity is characterized by increased TG
and ApoB-containing lipoproteins, decreased HDL-C levels,
and abnormal LDL-C composition [16,17]. Atherogenic dyslipi-
demia in obese subjects may be caused by a combination of
overproduction of very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) ApoB-
100, decreased catabolism of ApoB-containing particles, and
increased
catabolism
of
HDL-ApoA1
particles
[17].

abnormalities may be consequent on a global metabolic effect

of free fatty acids, promote free fatty acids into the liver, and

Both obesity and dyslipidemia are the major components
of the metabolic syndrome and are also identiﬁed as independ-
ent risk factors for CAD. Although strong association has been
found between obesity and dyslipidemia, there are also many
different aspects between the two conditions. Obesity is also
affected by genetic and environmental factors and their inter-
actions [49], involving excessive caloric intake, unhealthy life-
style, physical inactivity, social and economic forces, as well as
metabolic and endocrine abnormalities. Several genome-wide
association studies in multiple populations have identiﬁed
many loci associated with obesity [50–53]. In a recent study,
Kunej et al. [54] also collected a total of 1,736 obesity associ-
ated loci and created a freely available obesity database,
including 1,515 protein-coding genes and 221 microRNAs
(miRNAs) collected from four mammalian species: human, cat-
tle, rat, and mouse. These loci were integrated as orthologs on
comparative genomic views in human, cattle, and mouse. The
database and genomic views are freely available online at:
http://www.integratomics-time.com/fat_deposition.
Bioinfor-
matics analyses of the collected data revealed some potential
novel obesity related molecular markers which represent focal
points for testing more targeted hypotheses and designing
experiments
for
further
studies.
However,
some
loci
are
directly associated with both obesity and dyslipidemia [55–58].
Thus, the interrelationship between SNPs and obesity on se-
rum lipid levels is extremely complex and was overlooked. For
example, obesity-related genes play a role in the central regu-
lation of energy balance, but some of the genes have also a
role in the adipose tissue itself [59].
This study has several limitations. First, the levels of edu-
cation, weight, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the
percentages of subjects who consumed alcohol were higher in
high BMI than in normal BMI subjects, whereas the percen-
tages of subjects who smoked cigarettes were lower in high
BMI than in normal BMI subjects. Although sex, age, education
level, physical activity, blood pressure, alcohol consumption,
and cigarette smoking have been adjusted for the statistical
analysis, we could not completely eliminate the potential
effects of these factors on serum lipid levels among different
genotypes in both groups. Second, the diet was not adjusted
for the statistical analysis. In this study, however, the diet in
this isolated population is consistent throughout the year and
among individuals because of the Bai Ku Yao’s reliance on a
limited number of locally available food items. Their staple
food is corn gruel or corn tortillas. On ordinary days, they are
vegetarians [7–9]. Third, it is clearly established that serum
lipid
levels are
regulated
by multiple
environmental and
genetic factors, and their interactions [7–12]. Although we
have detected the interactions of 10 SNPs and high BMI on se-
rum lipid levels in this study, there are still many unmeasured
environmental
and
genetic
factors
and
their
interactions.
Fourth, the sample size of our study is a bit small. The GG
homozygous of rs505151 SNP was not detected in our study
population. Nowadays, a study sample of about 1,800 subjects
is relatively small to detect main effects, and replication is
required to avoid publication of chance ﬁndings. The chance
of false-positive or inconsistent ﬁndings might be even larger
for interactions, so an even larger study sample is generally
required. Finally, the study was carried out in the Bai Ku Yao
population, an isolated subgroup of the Yao minority in China.
No replication of the interactions between SNPs and high BMI
on serum lipid parameters was obtained in this independent
population. Thus, the observed associations and interactions
between these SNPs and serum lipid parameters in this iso-
lated ethnic subgroup may not be the major characteristics of
these conditions in the other ethnic groups.
5. Conclusions
Several SNPs in normal and high BMI subjects were associated
with serum lipid levels in the Guangxi Bai Ku Yao population.
The interactions between rs2066715, rs2070895, rs2000813,
rs1801133, rs3757354, rs505151, rs2016520, and rs5888 ge-
notypes and high BMI on serum lipid levels were also detected.
These results suggest that the differences in serum lipid levels
between normal and high BMI subjects might partly result
from different interactions of several SNPs and high BMI. How-
ever, large studies of populations with different ethnic origins
are required to conﬁrm these observations.
